summary: For Spokane’s July 4, 2026 reopening of the Great Northern Clocktower chimes, a parks employee made an AI-generated promotional flyer that closely resembled local artist Matthew Clinard’s commercially sold Clocktower sticker. The mayor’s office posted the flyer without identifying its synthetic origin, contrary to the city disclosure requirement described by its spokesperson; other city staff reportedly did not know how the parks employee had made it. Clinard publicly objected, after which the mayor’s office removed the image and apologised. City officials discussed policy reform and training. The parks employee said the prompt requested only a retro colour/style, so the exact image-production and training path is unknown; the visual overlap and missing recognition are evidenced without deciding copyright infringement. A separate police synthetic-dog-photo episode in the same article is not this Incident.

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: The city publicly distributed an AI-made Clocktower flyer without the required AI disclosure; this independently supports the disclosure-control failure. A contemporaneous report describes multiple striking one-to-one matches with an artist's earlier commercial sticker; the artist objected, and the city withdrew the flyer. These observations positively engage possible AI-mediated incorporation of an uncredited human contribution, but the model's source and any authorisation or attribution arrangements remain unresolved. Interested-party non-confirmation is not affirmative evidence that incorporation did not occur.

primary_classification.classification_basis: The city had an operative AI-disclosure requirement, yet the public flyer was published without the required disclosure.

secondary_classifications.classification_basis: The local newspaper documented one-to-one correspondence between distinctive features of the artist's earlier commercial sticker and the AI-generated flyer, including the clouds, trees, bushes, sun and palette. The artist objected and the city removed the uncredited image. This specific correspondence materially engages possible incorporation and human-contribution non-recognition. Neither the employee's attributed generic-style prompt nor unpublished production records establish independent generation; the actual source-to-output relationship and justified credit arrangement remain unresolved.

boundary_adjudication.material_engagement: A contemporaneous reporter described one-to-one correspondence in multiple independently specified, distinctive design elements between the earlier commercially available human-created sticker and the subsequently generated AI flyer. The artist objected; the city took it down and apologised. Such particularised observable evidence positively engages possible model-mediated human-contribution use and erasure, beyond generic thematic similarity.

boundary_adjudication.decisive_blocker: The exact mechanism linking the human-designed original and the generated flyer and any authorised attribution arrangement are not established. Lack of disclosure of an interested party's production trace cannot establish non-incorporation, while resemblance alone cannot certify actual incorporation.

Proprietary model internals or a vendor admission are not prerequisites. vigil_assessment.factual_basis: The City of Spokane’s July 1 release establishes the restored Clocktower-chimes event. The Spokesman-Review independently interviewed artist Matthew Clinard and city spokespeople, published the withdrawn flyer image, and reports one-to-one correspondence of the sticker’s clouds, trees, bushes, sun and palette with the generated flyer, with minor tower changes. Parks produced it; the mayor’s office distributed it without an AI notice, and city spokesperson Erin Hut described the absence of disclosure as a policy breach. The article says the image was removed and Clinard received an apology, and the cabinet began discussing policy reform; it does not show completed reforms. A parks spokesperson relayed the creator’s claim of a generic retro prompt, leaving the material pathway by which the sticker composition appeared in the output unresolved. This source establishes a close reported derivative visual result, not an intentional theft or a legal holding. The city policy PDF was identified but its full text could not be retrieved during the fresh search; the direct city-spokesperson account supports the operative disclosure requirement without inventing implementation telemetry. The same news report’s police photograph concerns a separate department and occurrence. The employee’s reported generic retro prompt does not establish training provenance or intentional copying.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: A public disclosure control did not become operative when an AI-made city flyer was released. Independently, a recognisable human creative contribution was flattened out of the public account of the generated design until its creator objected. The latter concerns contribution recognition, not a determination of infringement, training data lineage or intentional plagiarism. The removal and apology are bounded recovery, not proof that reforms were completed. Required city disclosure and missing creative-contribution recognition remain separate failures, without copyright or training-lineage adjudication. The city policy is a source-grounded occurrence duty without an admitted canonical match. Removal and apology are bounded recovery; model-development and runtime-agent duties concern different objects.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: One short-lived municipal flyer illustrates two non-equivalent boundaries: the city failed to disclose the synthetic medium to viewers, and the artist whose distinctive work materially appeared in the output was not recognised. Different evidence supports each mechanism, while the public correction limits observed harm.
